10.5. Proof of Theorem 40

If mm is even, we prove the theorem by induction over mm in steps of two. For m=0m=0 both sides of (31) are 11 (for m=2m=2 see examples 35 and 39). For m≥2m\geq 2 we obtain from propositions 78 and 82 that both sides obey the same recursion because OPENℰ∪(sj,ti)∖{(s1,t1),(si,ti),(sj,tj)})=ℰ∖{(s1,t1),(si,ti)}|tj=ti\mathcal{E}\cup(s_{j},t_{i})\setminus\{(s_{1},t_{1}),(s_{i},t_{i}),(s_{j},t_{j})\})=\mathcal{E}\setminus\{(s_{1},t_{1}),(s_{i},t_{i})\}|_{t_{j}=t_{i}}. The case of odd mm was proved in Lemma 77.

11. Appendix: A matrix identity of Amitsur-Levitzki type

11.1. The Amitsur-Levitzki theorem

Let RR be a commutative ring and let A1,…,A2​n∈Mn×n​(R)A_{1},\ldots,A_{2n}\in M_{n\times n}(R) be a set of 2​n2n square matrices with nn rows and columns. A famous theorem of Amitsur-Levitzki states that the complete antisymmetrisation of the product of 2​n2n matrices vanishes:

(89) ∑π∈Σ2​nsgn(π)Aπ⁡(1)⋯Aπ⁡(2​n)=0.\sum_{\pi\in\Sigma_{2n}}\mathrm{sgn}\,(\pi)A_{\pi(1)}\cdots A_{\pi(2n)}=0\ .

It was observed by Rosset [Ros76, Pro15] that this formula is equivalent to the identity Ω2​n=0\Omega^{2n}=0, where Ω\Omega is a certain n×nn\times n matrix whose entries are one-forms (see below). A by-product of the results of this paper is an explicit formula for the antisymmetrisation of 2​n−12n-1 such matrices.

11.2. Antisymmetrisation of kk matrices

More generally, given kk matrices Ai∈Mn×n​(R)A_{i}\in M_{n\times n}(R) as above, it is interesting to ask for a formula for the antisymmetrisation

[A1,…,Ak]=∑π∈Σksgn(π)Aπ⁡(1)⋯Aπ⁡(k).[A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}]=\sum_{\pi\in\Sigma_{k}}\mathrm{sgn}\,(\pi)A_{\pi(1)}\cdots A_{\pi(k)}\ .

The case k=2k=2 is simply the commutator [A1,A2]=A1​A2−A2​A1[A_{1},A_{2}]=A_{1}A_{2}-A_{2}A_{1}.

Following Definition 21 we choose any ordering on ordered pairs of elements in {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\} and define types ν=((i1,j1),…,(ik,jk))\nu=((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots,(i_{k},j_{k})) to be sets of kk distinct such pairs in the chosen order. Let Ω∈Mn×n​(R1)\Omega\in M_{n\times n}(R^{1}) be an n×nn\times n matrix whose entries are 11-forms in a differential graded algebra R∙=⨁n≥0RnR^{\bullet}=\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}R^{n} where R0=RR^{0}=R. Its kk-fold product Ωk∈Mn×n​(Rk)\Omega^{k}\in M_{n\times n}(R^{k}) is a matrix of kk-forms and may be expanded by type:

(90) Ωk=∑νFν​ην,\Omega^{k}=\sum_{\nu}F_{\nu}\eta_{\nu}\ ,

as in (58), where Fν∈Mn×n​(R)F_{\nu}\in M_{n\times n}(R) and ην=Ωi1​j1∧…∧Ωik​jk\eta_{\nu}=\Omega_{i_{1}j_{1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\Omega_{i_{k}j_{k}} if ν=((i1,j1),…,(ik,jk))\nu=((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots,(i_{k},j_{k})) (see Definition 21 (i​i)(ii) for the case k=2​n−1k=2n-1).

Proposition 83.

In the above notation we have

(91) [A1,…,Ak]=∑νFν​det((Ar)i​j)r,i​j∈ν,[A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}]=\sum_{\nu}F_{\nu}\det\Big((A_{r})_{ij}\Big)_{r,ij\in\nu}\ ,

where ((Ar)i​j)r,i​j∈ν((A_{r})_{ij})_{r,ij\in\nu} is the k×kk\times k matrix with entries (Ar)i​j(A_{r})_{ij} in row r=1,…,kr=1,\ldots,k and column (i,j)(i,j), where (i,j)(i,j) ranges over the kk elements in ν\nu in order.

Proof.

Following Rosset, consider the graded exterior algebra R∙=⋀⨁i=1kR​eiR^{\bullet}=\bigwedge\bigoplus^{k}_{i=1}Re_{i} where e1,…,eke_{1},\ldots,e_{k} are generators in degree 11. We have R0=RR^{0}=R and Rk=R​e1∧…∧ek.R^{k}=R\,e_{1}\wedge\ldots\wedge e_{k}. Consider the matrix

Ω=∑r=1kAr​er∈Mn×n​(R1).\Omega=\sum_{r=1}^{k}A_{r}e_{r}\quad\in\quad M_{n\times n}\left(R^{1}\right)\ .

Then by antisymmetry, we have

Ωk=[A1,…,Ak]​e1∧…∧ek.\Omega^{k}=[A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}]\,e_{1}\wedge\ldots\wedge e_{k}\ .

Now the (i,j)(i,j)th entry of Ω\Omega may be written

Ωi​j=(A1)i​j​e1+…+(Ak)i​j​ek.\Omega_{ij}=(A_{1})_{ij}e_{1}+\ldots+(A_{k})_{ij}e_{k}\ .

Substituting into ην\eta_{\nu} for ν=((i1,j1),…,(ik,jk))\nu=((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots,(i_{k},j_{k})) yields

ην​(e1,…,ek)=∑r1,…,rk=1k(Ar1)i1​j1​er1∧…∧(Ark)ik​jk​erk.\eta_{\nu}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{k})=\sum_{r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}=1}^{k}(A_{r_{1}})_{i_{1}j_{1}}e_{r_{1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge(A_{r_{k}})_{i_{k}j_{k}}e_{r_{k}}\ .

By antisymmetry again, this expression reduces to a determinant and (90) yields

Ωk=∑νFν​det((Ar)i​j)r=1,…,k,i​j∈ν​e1∧…∧ek.\Omega^{k}=\sum_{\nu}F_{\nu}\det\Big((A_{r})_{ij}\Big)_{r=1,\ldots,k,ij\in\nu}e_{1}\wedge\ldots\wedge e_{k}\ .

Comparing the coefficients of e1∧…∧eke_{1}\wedge\ldots\wedge e_{k} gives the result. ∎

It is an interesting question to find formulae for the coefficients FνF_{\nu} in (90), and hence for [A1,…,Ak][A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}]. The theorem of Amitsur-Levitzki is equivalent to the statement that all FνF_{\nu} vanish when k=2​nk=2n. The results obtained in this paper give an explicit formula in the case k=2​n−1.k=2n-1.

11.3. Antisymmetrisation of 2​n−12n-1 matrices of rank nn

Recall that the weight w⁡(ν)=(p¯​(ν),q¯​(ν))w(\nu)=({\underline{p}}(\nu),{\underline{q}}(\nu)) of ν\nu is defined by (see Definition 19)

p¯​(ν)=|{i:(i,j)∈ν}|,q¯​(ν)=|{j:(i,j)∈ν}|.{\underline{p}}(\nu)=|\{i:(i,j)\in\nu\}|\ ,\qquad{\underline{q}}(\nu)=|\{j:(i,j)\in\nu\}|\ .

The pairs in ν\nu have entries from 11 to nn, where nn is the rank of ν\nu.

Theorem 84.

The (i,j)(i,j)th component of the antisymmetrization of the 2​n−12n-1 generic matrices A1,A_{1}, …,\ldots, A2​n−1∈Mn×n​(R)A_{2n-1}\in M_{n\times n}(R) is given by

(92) [A1,…,A2​n−1]i​j=(−1)(n2)+s−1∑ν:p¯​(ν)−q¯​(ν)=e¯i−e¯jdet(Mν∅,s)(∏r=12​n−1(p¯(ν)r+δj,r−1)!)det((Ar)i​j)r,i​j∈ν,[A_{1},\ldots,A_{2n-1}]_{ij}=(-1)^{\binom{n}{2}+s-1}\sum_{\nu:{\underline{p}}(\nu)-{\underline{q}}(\nu)={\underline{e}}_{i}-{\underline{e}}_{j}}\det(M_{\nu}^{\emptyset,s})\,\Big(\prod_{r=1}^{2n-1}({\underline{p}}(\nu)_{r}+\delta_{j,r}-1)!\Big)\det\Big((A_{r})_{ij}\Big)_{r,ij\in\nu}\ ,

where ss is any number in {1,…,2​n}\{1,\ldots,2n\} (the formula does not depend on which one), the sum is over types ν\nu of rank nn, and the factorial of a negative number is defined to be 11. The matrix MνM_{\nu} and the notation Mν∅,sM_{\nu}^{\emptyset,s} are defined in Definition 21 (i)(i) and (i​i​i)(iii).

Proof.

Use propositions 17 (with B=InB=I_{n}) and 72, and substitute (19) into the formula for Ω2​n−1\Omega^{2n-1}. The result follows from Proposition 83. ∎

Example 85.

Let A,B,CA,B,C be three 2×22\times 2 matrices. The antisymmetrisation

[A,B,C]=A​B​C−B​A​C+B​C​A−C​B​A+C​A​B−A​C​B[A,B,C]=ABC-BAC+BCA-CBA+CAB-ACB

is given by determinants of the following 3×33\times 3 matrices (see Example 14 with B=I2B=I_{2}):

X1=(a11a12a21b11b12b21c11c12c21),X2=(a11a12a22b11b12b22c11c12c22),X3=(a11a21a22b11b21b22c11c21c22),X4=(a12a21a22b12b21b22c12c21c22)X_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}&a_{21}\\ b_{11}&b_{12}&b_{21}\\ c_{11}&c_{12}&c_{21}\\ \end{pmatrix}\ ,\ X_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}&a_{22}\\ b_{11}&b_{12}&b_{22}\\ c_{11}&c_{12}&c_{22}\\ \end{pmatrix}\ ,\ X_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{21}&a_{22}\\ b_{11}&b_{21}&b_{22}\\ c_{11}&c_{21}&c_{22}\\ \end{pmatrix}\ ,\ X_{4}=\begin{pmatrix}a_{12}&a_{21}&a_{22}\\ b_{12}&b_{21}&b_{22}\\ c_{12}&c_{21}&c_{22}\\ \end{pmatrix}

as

[A,B,C]=(2​detX1−detX4detX2−detX3detX1−2​detX4).[A,B,C]=\begin{pmatrix}2\det X_{1}-\det X_{4}&\det X_{2}\\ -\det X_{3}&\det X_{1}-2\det X_{4}\end{pmatrix}\ .
